articles.title: LA's $467 Million Housing Funding Round: How Measure ULA Money Is Being Used
articles.body_html:
Los Angeles is preparing to make approximately $467 million available for affordable housing construction, preservation, and stabilization through the second round of its Homes for LA funding program.

About $324 million of that total comes from Measure ULA, the city’s additional transfer tax on high-value real estate transactions.

The Los Angeles Housing Department expects its application portal to open October 13, 2026, although that date is tentative.

For property owners and investors, the announcement shows where a substantial portion of Measure ULA revenue is going and how the city is attempting to finance housing when construction and borrowing remain expensive.

What is the new Homes for LA funding round?

Homes for LA is a competitive funding program administered by the Los Angeles Housing Department.

The current round makes approximately $466.6 million available to support affordable housing development and preserve existing affordable properties.

Funding availability is not the same as completed housing. The announcement does not mean all the money has been spent, that every applicant will receive an award, or that funded projects will immediately begin construction.

Applicants must satisfy program requirements, compete for funding, and move through underwriting and approval. The path from funding authorization to occupied housing can take years.

Where does the $467 million come from?

Measure ULA accounts for approximately $324 million. The remaining resources come from other public funding sources, including affordable housing fees and regional housing programs.

Measure ULA was approved by Los Angeles voters in 2022 and began generating applicable property-transfer-tax revenue in April 2023.

Its purpose is to finance affordable housing and homelessness-prevention programs within the City of Los Angeles. This funding round illustrates how some of those revenues are being allocated.

What types of projects can receive funding?

The department identifies seven funding programs. Three focus on construction, three focus on preserving existing affordable housing, and one provides operating assistance intended to stabilize affordable properties.

The construction programs include conventional multifamily development and alternative ownership or governance models.

Preservation programs can address buildings where affordability is at risk, rehabilitation is necessary, or financial distress threatens operations.

These are different problems. A new building needs development capital. An aging building may need rehabilitation financing. An existing property with insufficient operating income may need a different intervention.

Why does preservation matter as much as construction?

Housing conversations often center on how many new apartments a city can build. That is important, but only part of the equation.

Los Angeles also has existing affordable properties facing rising insurance, maintenance, repair, and financing costs.

If those buildings deteriorate or become financially unstable, the city risks losing homes already serving lower-income residents.

Preserving existing affordable housing can sometimes be more efficient than replacing those units with new construction. That does not mean preservation is always the better investment. It means both approaches deserve scrutiny.

How does Measure ULA affect property sales?

Measure ULA imposes an additional transfer tax on qualifying transactions within the City of Los Angeles.

For transactions closing after June 30, 2026, the published thresholds are more than $5.4 million but less than $10.9 million at 4%, and $10.9 million or more at 5.5%. The city also imposes its existing base transfer tax, currently 0.45%.

Qualifying apartment buildings and commercial properties can be affected, not only expensive single-family houses. That is why describing Measure ULA exclusively as a mansion tax can be misleading.

Exemptions and other transaction-specific rules matter, so sellers should verify the applicable treatment before relying on a calculation.

What does the tax mean for a seller?

Consider a hypothetical $6 million property sale. Assuming the transaction is taxable and no exemption applies, the additional 4% ULA component would equal $240,000.

The separate 0.45% city base transfer tax would add $27,000. Those two city-level components total approximately $267,000, before other applicable transaction expenses and taxes.

A seller should not focus only on the gross sale price. Net proceeds after taxes, brokerage compensation, closing costs, debt repayment, and other obligations determine what the seller actually receives.

Those calculations should be completed before setting a pricing strategy.

Does Measure ULA affect multifamily investment?

Yes, particularly at higher transaction values. An investor buying above the applicable threshold should consider how the tax could affect a future sale and the projected return.

A five-year holding period may require different exit-cost assumptions from a transaction below the threshold.

The tax can also influence how buyers evaluate redevelopment opportunities or properties requiring major capital improvements.

But it would be too simplistic to attribute every investment decision to Measure ULA. Financing, rental income, insurance, property taxes, tenant regulations, construction costs, and market conditions also matter.

Is Measure ULA helping or hurting housing development?

There are competing perspectives. Supporters argue the tax creates dedicated resources for affordable housing and tenant stability. The new funding round is a concrete example of revenue being allocated.

Critics argue the additional transaction cost can discourage some high-value sales or make certain projects harder to finance.

I would separate two questions: Is the tax generating money for housing programs? Yes. Does that automatically establish that its overall economic effect is positive or negative? No.

A complete assessment needs to examine both program outcomes and effects on transactions and development.

Who can apply for the new funding?

This is not a general grant for homeowners remodeling a house or building a backyard ADU.

Homes for LA is structured around qualifying affordable housing projects and eligible sponsors. Depending on the program, applicants may include experienced affordable housing developers, nonprofits, community land trusts, and other qualifying entities.

Eligibility, underwriting, affordability requirements, and project-readiness standards vary. Applicants should review official term sheets and regulations.

The portal is tentatively scheduled to open October 13. Published reporting identifies November 13 as the sponsor application deadline and December 4 as the project application deadline. Verify final dates directly with LAHD.

What should property owners watch next?

I would focus on three developments: how much funding goes to new construction versus preservation, how quickly awards turn into construction, and what measurable results the city produces.

The City Council has called for quarterly reporting on implementation, including awards, expenditures, progress, and delays.

For investors, results could also show where affordable housing development is becoming more financially feasible.

An announced funding total is a starting point, not the final measure of success.

Frequently asked questions

How much money is available? Approximately $467 million, including about $324 million from Measure ULA.

When do applications open? Tentatively October 13, 2026, subject to confirmation by LAHD.

Is the funding only for new apartments? No. Construction, preservation, and operating assistance are included.

Does Measure ULA apply to every sale? No. It applies to qualifying City of Los Angeles transfers above the applicable thresholds, subject to exemptions.

Does the city tax apply in Beverly Hills or Santa Monica? Not automatically. Those are separate municipalities with their own applicable rules.

Can a homeowner use this for an ADU? This round is not a general-purpose homeowner ADU grant.

Paul's take

This round gives us another opportunity to evaluate Measure ULA based on actual results. The city is allocating substantial money, but the practical questions are which projects receive it, how many units are built or preserved, and how long it takes.

For property owners and investors, the tax itself also deserves attention. A transaction can look attractive based on gross sale price while producing a very different result after taxes and costs.

Understanding both sides of the equation is essential.

articles.title: Hollywood Burbank Airport's New Terminal: What Changes for Travelers on October 13
articles.body_html:
Hollywood Burbank Airport is preparing to open its new $1.3 billion passenger terminal on October 13, 2026, replacing facilities that have served the airport for decades.

The new terminal contains approximately 355,000 square feet, 14 gates, updated security and baggage facilities, restaurants, retail, and a new parking structure.

The airport held a ribbon-cutting ceremony October 5 ahead of the scheduled public opening.

For Los Angeles residents, this is one of the region’s significant transportation openings of the year. It also changes something practical: where travelers need to go.

What is the new Hollywood Burbank Airport terminal?

The project is known as Elevate BUR. It replaces older passenger facilities with a modern building intended to address safety, accessibility, and operational limitations.

The airport authority describes it as a safety project rather than a major flight-capacity expansion.

The new terminal retains 14 gates, the same number as the previous facility.

The goal is better passenger circulation, updated systems, and greater separation between the terminal and runways, not simply making the airport bigger.

When does the new terminal open?

The scheduled public opening is Tuesday, October 13, 2026. The airport celebrated the project with an October 5 ribbon-cutting ceremony.

Travelers should verify directions, parking arrangements, and terminal access before leaving home. Major airport transitions can involve temporary traffic changes.

Where is the new terminal located?

The replacement terminal is in the northeastern portion of the airport.

Official traveler guidance identifies the address as 2827 North Hollywood Way, with an entrance at Hollywood Way and Winona Avenue.

That is a meaningful change from the old terminal arrangement.

Regular passengers should not assume their usual driving route or pickup location is unchanged. The same advice applies to rideshare users and anyone arranging a pickup.

What will be different inside?

Passengers will use a consolidated facility with a central ticketing hall, security checkpoint, and baggage claim instead of navigating separate terminal areas.

The design includes updated technology, improved accessibility, and additional amenities.

The airport authority describes a larger environment with more shopping and dining options.

For occasional travelers and visitors, clearer circulation may be as useful as the architectural improvements.

What about parking?

Parking arrangements change with the terminal opening. According to the airport’s published guidance, parking structure and valet operations relocate to the new terminal on October 13.

Lot E is scheduled to close permanently that day. Lot C closed in August as part of the transition.

The new parking structure sits near the terminal entrance.

Check current availability, prices, and directions instead of relying on previous habits. A familiar parking route may no longer work.

Can you still take Metrolink to Burbank Airport?

Yes. Hollywood Burbank Airport is served by two Metrolink stations.

Burbank Airport–South is on the Ventura County Line. Burbank Airport–North is on the Antelope Valley Line.

Metrolink’s updated guidance says South station passengers can connect to the new terminal by airport shuttle. From North station, travelers can walk about half a mile or use an on-demand airport shuttle.

For residents with convenient rail access, that can be an alternative to driving and paying for parking. Confirm shuttle instructions before traveling.

Will the airport have more flights?

The replacement terminal does not automatically mean more flights.

The airport authority specifically characterizes Elevate BUR as a safety and modernization effort rather than a capacity expansion.

The terminal maintains the existing 14-gate configuration. Future airline service depends on airline decisions, demand, and operating conditions.

It would be misleading to present this opening as an announcement of substantial new flight capacity.

Why did the airport need a replacement?

The older terminal was built under standards that differ from current airport design requirements.

The replacement is intended to improve runway separation, accessibility, seismic performance, and passenger operations.

Those improvements may be less visible than new restaurants or a dramatic roofline, but they are central to the project.

A modern airport must work safely and efficiently for passengers, employees, airlines, and emergency services.

What does the new building look like?

The selected design is called The Icon. Its distinctive feature is a sweeping roof canopy extending toward the entrance and adjacent parking structure.

The design references Southern California’s entertainment industry and creates a recognizable arrival experience.

That is appropriate for an airport serving Burbank, Hollywood, and surrounding entertainment and production communities.

Transportation facilities also function as civic architecture. For many visitors, an airport is their first impression of a region.

Why does this matter to people living in Los Angeles?

Transportation access is part of neighborhood convenience.

Someone living in Studio City, Sherman Oaks, Toluca Lake, Burbank, or Glendale may evaluate airport access differently from someone living in Santa Monica or the South Bay.

For some households, Burbank is already an attractive alternative to LAX because of its location.

The new terminal may improve the experience, although convenience still depends on location, route, airline, and schedule.

Transportation belongs in conversations about where people want to live because it affects everyday decisions.

Could the terminal affect nearby real estate?

Major transportation investments can change how people perceive an area, but I would not claim the terminal automatically increases nearby home values.

Airport proximity involves tradeoffs. Some buyers value convenient flights and employment access; others are sensitive to noise and traffic.

A house directly under a flight path presents different considerations from a condominium several miles away.

Buyers should evaluate actual noise exposure and transportation patterns rather than assuming airport proximity is always a benefit or always a drawback.

What should travelers do before their first visit?

Confirm the new address, review updated parking information, and check pickup or drop-off instructions.

Anyone using Metrolink should check current shuttle directions. Travelers should allow extra time during the initial transition, especially if they have not used the airport recently.

The most important change is simple: do not assume the route you used last month is still the correct route.

Frequently asked questions

When does the new terminal open? The airport has scheduled October 13, 2026. Verify the actual opening before travel.

Where is the new terminal? 2827 North Hollywood Way, near Hollywood Way and Winona Avenue.

How many gates are there? Fourteen, unchanged from the previous terminal.

Is there new parking? Yes, and parking operations are changing.

Can I take Metrolink? Yes, via connections to the South and North airport stations.

Does this mean more flights? Not necessarily. The project is a safety and modernization effort.

Paul's take

I see this as an important quality-of-life improvement for the eastern San Fernando Valley and nearby communities.

People tend to focus on the home itself when comparing neighborhoods, but transportation matters too.

How easily can you reach work? How much time do you spend driving? Is public transit useful? How convenient is the nearest airport?

The terminal will not change everyone’s daily routine, but for residents who use Burbank regularly, it is a meaningful infrastructure improvement.

articles.title: Mel's Drive-In Could Be Replaced by 138 Apartments: What's Proposed in Santa Monica
articles.body_html:
A proposed eight-story development could replace one of Santa Monica’s most recognizable examples of midcentury roadside architecture.

The owner of the property at 1670 Lincoln Boulevard, currently occupied by Mel’s Drive-In, has submitted plans for a mixed-use building containing 138 apartments, ground-floor commercial space, and parking.

The proposal would demolish the restaurant building, originally constructed in 1959 as the Penguin Coffee Shop.

The redevelopment has not been completed or approved, and preservation advocates are pursuing local landmark designation.

The story raises two questions: how should Santa Monica accommodate more housing, and what happens when a housing proposal involves a building with architectural and cultural significance?

What is proposed at 1670 Lincoln Boulevard?

The property owner, ValueRock Realty, filed an application for an eight-story mixed-use development.

The proposal includes 138 studio, one-bedroom, and two-bedroom apartments, approximately 5,667 square feet of ground-floor commercial space, and parking for 123 vehicles.

Plans also include a rooftop deck and central courtyard. Ottinger Architects is responsible for the proposed design.

These details describe the current proposal, not final approvals or a guaranteed construction program.

Will Mel’s Drive-In be demolished?

The current redevelopment proposal calls for demolition of the restaurant building. That does not make demolition inevitable.

The project faces applicable review and approval processes. There is also an active effort to obtain historic landmark designation.

The Santa Monica Conservancy and Los Angeles Conservancy have supported preservation.

According to preservation organizations, a landmark hearing is scheduled for December 14, 2026. The outcome could influence what happens next.

Why is the building historically significant?

The restaurant originally opened in 1959 as the Penguin Coffee Shop.

It was designed by Armet & Davis, a firm associated with Southern California’s Googie style.

Googie architecture is known for expressive rooflines, prominent signage, extensive glass, and design elements reflecting midcentury optimism and automobile culture.

These buildings were designed to attract attention from passing drivers. The Penguin’s architecture and signage made it recognizable along Lincoln Boulevard.

The property later served other uses before operating as Mel’s Drive-In. For preservation advocates, the concern is losing a surviving example of regional architectural history, not simply another restaurant.

What is Googie architecture?

Googie is a modernist commercial architectural style associated with postwar Southern California.

It often features dramatic angles, large windows, expressive signs, and references to technology, movement, or the Space Age.

Coffee shops, diners, bowling alleys, and roadside businesses used the style to stand out.

That makes these buildings part of the region’s commercial history, but creates preservation challenges: many occupy valuable commercial sites along major corridors.

The visibility that made the buildings successful can also make the land attractive for redevelopment.

Why is this site attractive for housing?

The property is near Lincoln and Olympic boulevards, close to the Santa Monica Freeway and a corridor that has seen substantial multifamily development.

The proposed project sits south of a recently completed mixed-use building at 1650 Lincoln Boulevard.

Urbanize LA reports multiple housing projects completed along Lincoln Boulevard during the past decade.

This is not an isolated proposal to add housing to an unchanged street. It is part of a broader pattern of redevelopment along a major Santa Monica corridor.

How much affordable housing is proposed?

The current application identifies 14 apartments intended for very low-, low-, and moderate-income households.

The project seeks density-bonus incentives and other regulatory allowances associated with income-restricted housing.

The precise affordability mix, income limits, and final project conditions should be checked against city approval documents.

A project containing 138 apartments is not necessarily a project containing 138 affordable apartments. That distinction matters when evaluating its effect on housing access.

Could the development help housing supply?

Yes, if it proceeds. The proposed building would add a substantial number of apartments to a relatively small commercial site.

New residents could live near employment, retail, restaurants, and regional transportation. Additional households may also support nearby businesses.

But those benefits do not guarantee that the project solves affordability challenges.

New construction is expensive. Eventual rents, financing, and market conditions will determine how the building competes with existing housing.

What is the preservation argument?

Preservation advocates argue the building has architectural value independent of its current restaurant use.

They emphasize the original design, distinctive signage, and place in Santa Monica history. They also point to examples where historic buildings were incorporated into larger projects.

Could this site accommodate additional housing while preserving some or all of the structure? It is worth investigating, but not every alternative is technically or financially feasible.

Structural condition, site configuration, code requirements, costs, and development capacity all matter.

What is the argument for redevelopment?

Santa Monica faces substantial housing demand, and commercial corridors can offer opportunities for additional residents.

A relatively low-density commercial property may support far more housing than exists today.

From that perspective, the question is whether preserving one historic building should outweigh the opportunity to add more than 100 homes.

That is a legitimate policy consideration. It does not erase the building’s architectural value.

It illustrates the tension between preserving neighborhood character and increasing housing supply.

Could both objectives be accommodated?

Potentially, but no particular alternative should be assumed feasible without design and financial analysis.

A project might preserve a historic structure while adding construction elsewhere on the parcel. Other developments have done something similar.

Whether that works here depends on site dimensions, building configuration, parking, access, structure, and economics.

Preservation groups have identified examples in Santa Monica, but those examples do not prove the same approach works at 1670 Lincoln Boulevard.

What does this mean for nearby property owners?

Large redevelopment proposals can change how buyers perceive a neighborhood.

Some welcome housing, new retail, and investment. Others worry about construction, height, traffic, or losing a familiar landmark.

Effects depend on proximity. A condominium overlooking the site has different considerations from a house several blocks away.

I would not claim this proposal automatically increases or decreases nearby property values. The relationship between the project and each property matters.

What should buyers investigate near Lincoln Boulevard?

Start with surrounding land use. What is already under construction? Which parcels have active applications? What zoning applies to neighboring lots?

Are historic preservation issues involved? How much of the street may change in coming years?

These questions are particularly relevant for condominium buyers who value a current view or streetscape without realizing adjacent parcels may be redeveloped.

The condition of a neighborhood today is not necessarily its permanent condition.

Does this show Santa Monica is becoming denser?

It is another example of development pressure along commercial corridors.

Santa Monica has limited land area and demand for housing near jobs and amenities. That creates incentives to redevelop some lower-density sites.

Density is not distributed evenly. Some neighborhoods remain predominantly low-rise residential, while major corridors accommodate larger buildings.

Lincoln Boulevard is one place where that difference is visible.

What happens next?

Watch two processes: city review of the proposed 138-unit project and the historic landmark nomination.

The preservation hearing is scheduled for December 14, 2026.

A landmark decision, project redesign, entitlement approval, or construction announcement could justify updating this article.

For now, the redevelopment is proposed, the building has not been demolished, and the final outcome remains uncertain.

Frequently asked questions

Is Mel’s Drive-In closing? The application proposes demolition, but a confirmed closure or demolition date has not been established in the reviewed sources.

How many apartments are proposed? 138.

Where is the property? 1670 Lincoln Boulevard in Santa Monica.

How old is the building? It originally opened in 1959.

Is it a designated landmark? A nomination is pending; nomination is not the same as designation.

When is the landmark hearing? Preservation groups identify December 14, 2026.

Is the project approved? The current reporting describes a submitted proposal, not a final approval.

Paul's take

Both sides of this proposal raise legitimate considerations. Santa Monica needs housing, but buildings like the former Penguin Coffee Shop contribute to Southern California’s architectural identity.

I would not automatically conclude preservation should prevent redevelopment. I also would not assume demolition is the only way to create housing.

What alternatives are physically possible? What would they cost? How much housing could each produce? Which architectural features could be retained?

For buyers and owners, neighborhood change is about more than new buildings. It also involves deciding which parts of local history to preserve.
